items.stem: Which term describes media organisations, products and platforms that operate across national borders?
items.answer: Global media
items.markingKey: Global media: media organisations, products and platforms that operate across national borders. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “localisation”, and give one example.
items.answer: Adapting global media formats to local audiences. Example: a local version of an international talent show.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (adapting global media formats to local audiences); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a local version of an international talent show. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “global media” and “contra-flow”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Global media: media organisations, products and platforms that operate across national borders (e.g. a streaming service available in 190 countries). Contra-flow: media products flowing from non-Western countries to the West and elsewhere (e.g. Bollywood films and K-dramas watched worldwide).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A local film industry in Auckland struggles to compete as cinemas show mainly Hollywood films, which have much bigger marketing budgets. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Pluralism: media success reflects audience choice in a competitive market: Hollywood dominates where audiences prefer it, while local and non-Western producers can and do compete when they meet audience demand.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A local film industry in Manila struggles to compete as cinemas show mainly Hollywood films, which have much bigger marketing budgets. Explain how a transformationalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Transformationalism: global media are changing cultures, but flows are multi-directional and local cultures adapt global products (Thussu).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Mohammed, a sociology student, is designing a project on how young people use foreign media to shape their identities. Evaluate the use of field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; they take place in a natural setting, so behaviour is more realistic than in a laboratory. Limitations: they are hard to repeat exactly because conditions in the real world change; participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how young people use foreign media to shape their identities but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “contra-flow”?
items.answer: Media products flowing from non-Western countries to the West and elsewhere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: media products flowing from non-Western countries to the West and elsewhere. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “localisation” and “media imperialism”.
items.answer: Localisation: adapting global media formats to local audiences. Media imperialism: the domination of global media by Western, especially American, corporations and content.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Box-office statistics for a country near Manila are shown below. Table: share of cinema box-office takings in a country (%) | 2000 | 2022. US films | 66% | 61%. Domestic films | 20% | 32%. Other foreign films | 14% | 7%. By how many percentage points did the figure for US films change between 2000 and 2022?
items.answer: -5 percentage points
items.markingKey: 61 − 66 = -5 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Dhaka wants to research the origin of films shown in cinemas. Explain one strength of using content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Media content from different decades can be compared to measure change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant strength; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the origin of films shown in cinemas. [2]

items.stem: A sociologist in Auckland wants to research how young people use foreign media to shape their identities. Explain two limitations of using semi-structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. Interviewer bias may still affect answers. 2. Samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how young people use foreign media to shape their identities. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes Habermas’s term for a space where citizens can debate public issues freely and rationally?
items.answer: Public sphere
items.markingKey: Public sphere: Habermas’s term for a space where citizens can debate public issues freely and rationally. [1]

items.stem: Which term describes Habermas’s term for a space where citizens can debate public issues freely and rationally?
items.answer: Public sphere
items.markingKey: Public sphere: Habermas’s term for a space where citizens can debate public issues freely and rationally. [1]

items.stem: What is the difference between “digital public sphere” and “infotainment”?
items.answer: Digital public sphere: online spaces where citizens discuss public issues. Infotainment: media content that mixes information with entertainment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: Residents of Cairo use an online forum to debate a proposed motorway; the forum attracts thousands of comments, but many are abusive and few come from older residents. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: there is no single public sphere, only fragmented spaces and spectacles; reality and image blur.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Mateo, a sociology student, is designing a project on how people take part in online political debate. Explain one strength and one limitation of using structured interviews for this study.
items.answer: Strength: answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitation: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers.
items.markingKey: For each: 1 mark identified; 1 mark explained in the context of how people take part in online political debate. [4]

items.stem: Briefly explain Fraser’s view that there are many counter-publics, not one public sphere.
items.answer: Fraser argued excluded groups such as women created their own counter-public spheres.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the idea; 1 mark for developing it: Fraser argued excluded groups such as women created their own counter-public spheres. [2]

items.stem: Residents of Cape Town use an online forum to debate a proposed motorway; the forum attracts thousands of comments, but many are abusive and few come from older residents. Explain how a liberal feminist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Liberal feminism: excluded groups form counter-publics, and new media give them new spaces to be heard (Fraser).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: During an election in Karachi, the most-watched TV news programme spends more time on candidates’ clothes and personal lives than on their policies. Compare how pluralist and liberal feminist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: diverse media and new digital spaces allow many voices to be heard, sustaining democratic debate. Liberal feminism: excluded groups form counter-publics, and new media give them new spaces to be heard (Fraser).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a method of systematically counting and categorising the content of media texts?
items.answer: Content analysis
items.markingKey: Content analysis: a method of systematically counting and categorising the content of media texts. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “denotation”, and give one example.
items.answer: The literal, obvious meaning of a sign. Example: a picture of a dove shows a white bird.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the literal, obvious meaning of a sign); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a picture of a dove shows a white bird. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “denotation” and “semiology”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Denotation: the literal, obvious meaning of a sign (e.g. a picture of a dove shows a white bird). Semiology: the study of signs and the meanings they convey (e.g. analysing what a red rose in an advert signifies).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Leila records every advert shown in two hours of evening television in Hanoi and counts how many show women at home and how many show women at work. Suggest how an interpretivist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Interpretivism: counting ignores meaning; qualitative methods such as semiology and thematic analysis reveal how texts create meaning, and audience research shows interpretation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A research team asks groups of viewers in Dubai to write their own news report on a riot, using photographs taken from real TV coverage. Explain how a positivist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Positivism: content analysis is useful because it is systematic, quantitative and reliable, allowing comparisons and generalisations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A researcher analyses a perfume advert from Lagos, arguing that the gold colours, silk sheets and soft lighting connote luxury, desire and femininity. Compare how neo-Marxist and positivist sociologists might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: research should uncover the ideology hidden in media texts, for example how signs naturalise dominant values (Barthes, GUMG). Positivism: content analysis is useful because it is systematic, quantitative and reliable, allowing comparisons and generalisations.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Tariq, a sociology student, is designing a project on how teenagers interpret music videos. Evaluate the use of laboratory experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the procedure is standardised, so the experiment can be repeated to check reliability; the researcher controls variables, so cause and effect relationships can be identified. Limitations: the artificial setting means people may not behave as they would in real life, so validity is low; it is impossible to control all the variables that affect human behaviour. Theory: laboratory experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teenagers interpret music videos but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Muscat wants to research the representation of migrants in newspapers. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; the interviewer can explain unclear questions, so fewer answers are spoiled. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the representation of migrants in newspapers but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a method of systematically counting and categorising the content of media texts?
items.answer: Content analysis
items.markingKey: Content analysis: a method of systematically counting and categorising the content of media texts. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “denotation”.
items.answer: The literal, obvious meaning of a sign.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the literal, obvious meaning of a sign. [1]

items.stem: Explain Barthes’s argument that signs carry denotative and connotative meanings, and myths make ideology seem natural, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Barthes analysed a magazine cover of a black soldier saluting the French flag as a myth supporting colonialism. Criticism: Interpretations of signs are subjective.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Distinguish between “connotation” and “denotation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Connotation: the cultural and symbolic meanings associated with a sign (e.g. a dove connotes peace). Denotation: the literal, obvious meaning of a sign (e.g. a picture of a dove shows a white bird).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Samuel, a sociology student, is designing a project on the representation of migrants in newspapers. Explain one limitation of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: They are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the representation of migrants in newspapers. [2]

items.stem: Study the following extract (Source A) from a report on research carried out in Accra. “A researcher in Istanbul studied 300 newspaper articles about migrants using a coding schedule. 62% of articles used words such as “flood” or “wave”; 15% quoted a migrant. A semiological analysis of the front-page photographs found migrants were usually shown in large, faceless crowds.” (a) Explain how a neo-Marxist sociologist might interpret the findings in Source A. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that content analysis is the most useful method for studying media representations.
items.answer: (a) The findings suggest the media construct migrants as a threat, a myth (Barthes) that diverts attention from inequality and reinforces dominant ideology. (b) For: The source shows content analysis produces clear, reliable, comparable figures; combined with semiology it reveals meaning. Against: Coding categories may reflect the researcher’s views; counting does not reveal meaning or audience interpretation; semiology is subjective; audience research (Morley, Philo) is also needed. Also consider how far a single study using content analysis can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the findings in the source. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Explain two strengths of semiology as a method for researching the media.
items.answer: Reveals hidden meanings and ideology; analyses images as well as words; qualitative depth; shows how myths naturalise dominant values (Barthes).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): one or two simple points, limited sociological knowledge. Level 2 (4-6): explained points using some concepts, studies or theories. Level 3 (7-8): two well-explained, developed points with accurate concepts, studies or theories, clearly applied to the question. Creditworthy: Reveals hidden meanings and ideology; analyses images as well as words; qualitative depth; shows how myths naturalise dominant values (Barthes). [8]

items.stem: Yusuf is planning a study of the representation of migrants in newspapers. Evaluate the use of official statistics for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; they show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the representation of migrants in newspapers but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the domination of global media by Western, especially American, corporations and content?
items.answer: Media imperialism
items.markingKey: Media imperialism: the domination of global media by Western, especially American, corporations and content. [1]

items.stem: State one example of non-Western media reaching global audiences.
items.answer: Japanese anime.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. Japanese anime. [1]

items.stem: McLuhan argued that electronic media create a global village. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: McLuhan argued the medium itself changes how people experience the world. Criticism: Access is unequal and global media can divide as well as unite.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Hyperglobalism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: The table shows the share of cinema takings by film origin in one country. Table: share of cinema box-office takings in a country (%) | 2000 | 2022. US films | 67% | 58%. Domestic films | 23% | 33%. Other foreign films | 10% | 9%. By how many percentage points did the figure for US films change between 2000 and 2022?
items.answer: -9 percentage points
items.markingKey: 58 − 67 = -9 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: Box-office statistics for a country near Toronto are shown below. Table: share of cinema box-office takings in a country (%) | 2000 | 2022. US films | 69% | 62%. Domestic films | 15% | 21%. Other foreign films | 16% | 17%. (a) Using the data, identify the group with the highest figure for 2022. (b) Calculate the gap between US films and Other foreign films in 2000 and in 2022, and state whether it narrowed or widened.
items.answer: (a) US films (62%). (b) 2000: 53 percentage points; 2022: 45 percentage points; the gap narrowed.
items.markingKey: (a) US films, 62%. [1] (b) 1 mark each gap (53 and 45); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3]

items.stem: The table shows the share of cinema takings by film origin in one country. Table: share of cinema box-office takings in a country (%) | 2000 | 2022. US films | 70% | 65%. Domestic films | 19% | 29%. Other foreign films | 11% | 6%. (a) Calculate the change, in percentage points, for Domestic films between 2000 and 2022. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that media imperialism is declining.
items.answer: (a) 29 − 19 = +10 percentage points. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Domestic films; the figure fell for US films, Other foreign films; US films had the highest figure for 2022. Contra-flows from other non-Western producers. Qualifications: US films still dominate; streaming is not included; domestic films may copy Hollywood styles or be co-produced by US firms. The data also come from official statistics of 3 films in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 19 and 29; 1 mark for +10 percentage points (sign or “rise/fall” needed). [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes Habermas’s term for the decline of the public sphere as commercial media turn citizens into passive consumers?
items.answer: Refeudalisation
items.markingKey: Refeudalisation: Habermas’s term for the decline of the public sphere as commercial media turn citizens into passive consumers. [1]

items.stem: Explain what Habermas meant by the public sphere.
items.answer: A space between private life and the state where citizens could debate public issues freely and rationally, forming public opinion, e.g. coffee houses, newspapers and pamphlets.
items.markingKey: 1 mark meaning; 1 mark development; 1 mark example. [3]

items.stem: A sociologist in Nairobi wants to research how people take part in online political debate. Explain one limitation of using case studies for this research.
items.answer: One case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of how people take part in online political debate. [2]

items.stem: Grace, a sociology student, is designing a project on the content of TV election coverage. Explain two limitations of using official statistics for this research.
items.answer: 1. Interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. 2. They show patterns but not the meanings or reasons behind them.
items.markingKey: For each limitation: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to the content of TV election coverage. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful unstructured interviews are for studying how people take part in online political debate.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; they produce rich, detailed qualitative data that gives verstehen (an empathetic understanding). Limitations: they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare; the interviewer may lead the interviewee or interpret answers selectively (interviewer bias). Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how people take part in online political debate but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes the list of categories a researcher uses to classify media content in a content analysis?
items.answer: Coding schedule
items.markingKey: Coding schedule: the list of categories a researcher uses to classify media content in a content analysis. [1]

items.stem: State one limitation of content analysis.
items.answer: Large samples are time-consuming to code.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a valid point, e.g. large samples are time-consuming to code. [1]

items.stem: Explain two strengths of content analysis as a method for studying the media.
items.answer: Quantitative, systematic and reliable (repeatable with the same coding schedule); large samples; cheap and accessible; no ethical problems with participants; can show changes over time.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained strength. [4]

items.stem: Explain Glasgow University Media Group’s argument that systematic content analysis reveals bias in television news, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: They used content analysis and thematic analysis to study the language and images of news. Criticism: Critics argue their categories reflected their own assumptions.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Diego found this account of a study (Source A) while revising. “A researcher in Santiago studied 300 newspaper articles about migrants using a coding schedule. 62% of articles used words such as “flood” or “wave”; 15% quoted a migrant. A semiological analysis of the front-page photographs found migrants were usually shown in large, faceless crowds.” (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying representations of migrants. (b) Explain how a neo-Marxist sociologist might interpret the findings in Source A.
items.answer: (a) Counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. (b) The findings suggest the media construct migrants as a threat, a myth (Barthes) that diverts attention from inequality and reinforces dominant ideology.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the findings in the source. [3]

items.stem: A researcher in Colombo studies the colours, objects and camera angles in a car advert to uncover what they symbolise. Which approach to researching the media is being used?
items.answer: Semiology
items.markingKey: Semiology: analysing signs and their connotations. [1]

items.stem: Nadia is planning a study of how teenagers interpret music videos. Explain two strengths of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: 1. Variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom. 2. Participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally.
items.markingKey: For each strength: 1 mark identified, 1 mark explained and applied to how teenagers interpret music videos. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying the representation of migrants in newspapers.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are usually free and readily available, saving time and money. Limitations: definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult; they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the representation of migrants in newspapers but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

A semiological analysis of the front-page photographs found migrants were usually shown in large, faceless crowds.” (a) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying representations of migrants. items.answer: Closed questions impose the researcher’s categories and cannot explore the meanings behind answers, which lowers validity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the origin of films shown in cinemas. [2]

items.stem: Hana, a sociology student, is designing a project on the origin of films shown in cinemas. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media. Limitations: counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context; it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the origin of films shown in cinemas but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain what Habermas meant by the public sphere. (b) Explain two ways in which new media might revive the public sphere.
items.answer: (a) A space between private life and the state where citizens could debate public issues freely and rationally, forming public opinion, e.g. coffee houses, newspapers and pamphlets. items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark meaning; 1 mark development; 1 mark example. [3] (b) 2 marks for each explained way. [4]

items.stem: During an election in Manila, the most-watched TV news programme spends more time on candidates’ clothes and personal lives than on their policies. Suggest how a pluralist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Pluralism: diverse media and new digital spaces allow many voices to be heard, sustaining democratic debate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Residents of Lisbon use an online forum to debate a proposed motorway; the forum attracts thousands of comments, but many are abusive and few come from older residents. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: there is no single public sphere, only fragmented spaces and spectacles; reality and image blur.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Hanoi wants to research the content of TV election coverage. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the content of TV election coverage but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a qualitative analysis of the underlying themes and meanings in media texts?
items.answer: Thematic analysis
items.markingKey: Thematic analysis: a qualitative analysis of the underlying themes and meanings in media texts. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “coding schedule”.
items.answer: The list of categories a researcher uses to classify media content in a content analysis.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: the list of categories a researcher uses to classify media content in a content analysis. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): denotation refers to the hidden cultural meaning of a sign. Reason (R): other researchers can repeat it using the same coding schedule. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: A is false but R is true
items.markingKey: A is false: “denotation refers to the hidden cultural meaning of a sign.” is incorrect; R is a true statement. [1]

items.stem: Distinguish between “semiology” and “thematic analysis”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Semiology: the study of signs and the meanings they convey (e.g. analysing what a red rose in an advert signifies). Thematic analysis: a qualitative analysis of the underlying themes and meanings in media texts (e.g. identifying how migrants are framed in news stories).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Mei found this account of a study (Source A) while revising. “A researcher in Lagos studied 300 newspaper articles about migrants using a coding schedule. 62% of articles used words such as “flood” or “wave”; 15% quoted a migrant. A semiological analysis of the front-page photographs found migrants were usually shown in large, faceless crowds.” (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying representations of migrants.
items.answer: (a) 1. 62% of articles used words such as “flood” or “wave”. 2. Only 15% quoted a migrant. (b) Coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2]

items.stem: A researcher in Nairobi studies the colours, objects and camera angles in a car advert to uncover what they symbolise. Which approach to researching the media is being used?
items.answer: Semiology
items.markingKey: Semiology: analysing signs and their connotations. [1]

items.stem: A researcher analyses a perfume advert from Hanoi, arguing that the gold colours, silk sheets and soft lighting connote luxury, desire and femininity. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might evaluate this research.
items.answer: Postmodernism: texts have no fixed meaning; audiences create many meanings, so no method can uncover a single true reading.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Tomás, a sociology student, is designing a project on how teenagers interpret music videos. Evaluate the use of structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how teenagers interpret music videos but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Jonas is planning a study of the representation of migrants in newspapers. Evaluate the use of content analysis for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; it allows representations to be compared over time or between different media. Limitations: it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it; counting images or words may miss their deeper meaning and context. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the representation of migrants in newspapers but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
